nameStory: Cave Swallows get their name from their strong preference for nesting and roosting in caves and sinkholes, unlike their cliff-dwelling cousins. While most swallows build their mud nests under bridges or barn eaves, these birds seek out the cool, sheltered environment of natural caves. This cave-loving habit makes them quite specialized in their habitat choices compared to other North American swallows.
description: The Cave Swallow is a medium-sized swallow with a distinctive square-shaped tail that sets it apart from many of its relatives. These aerial acrobats are native to warmer regions of the Americas but occasionally show up as vagrants along the New England coast, especially during fall migration. They're skilled insect hunters that spend most of their time swooping and diving through the air. Like other swallows, they have streamlined bodies built for catching flying insects on the wing.

idTips.label: Square tail
idTips.description: The tail appears distinctly square or slightly notched when spread, rather than the deeply forked tail of many other swallows

idTips.label: Rusty rump patch
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive rufous or rusty-colored patch on the rump that's visible when the bird banks and turns in flight

idTips.label: Pale throat
idTips.description: The throat appears notably pale or whitish, contrasting with darker head markings

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with quick, erratic wingbeats and sudden direction changes while hunting insects over open areas

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Medium-sized swallow with a sturdy, compact body that appears less streamlined than some of its relatives

habitat: In New England, Cave Swallows are extremely rare vagrants typically spotted along the coast during migration periods. They're most likely to be seen over open areas near water, beaches, or coastal marshes where flying insects are abundant. Unlike resident swallows, they won't be found nesting here but may appear briefly while following weather systems or during dispersal from their normal range.

seasonality.spring: Very rarely seen during spring migration, though any coastal sighting would be noteworthy and worth reporting to birding communities.
seasonality.summer: Not expected in New England during summer as they breed much farther south in places like Texas and Florida.
seasonality.fall: The most likely time to spot a vagrant Cave Swallow, typically from late September through November along the coast during migration.
seasonality.winter: Extremely unlikely to be seen in winter, as most birds head to warmer climates and New England's harsh conditions would be unsuitable.

funFact: Cave Swallows have been expanding their range northward by adapting to nest under highway overpasses and culverts, essentially treating these human-made structures as artificial caves and allowing them to colonize areas far from natural cave systems.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the much more common Cliff Swallow, but Cave Swallows have a square tail (not forked), a rusty rump patch, and a paler throat. Remember: 'Cave has a square' - the square tail is your best field mark to separate it from other swallows.
contextualKnowledge: Cave Swallows are considered accidental visitors to New England, meaning any sighting is quite special and worth documenting with photos if possible. With only about 30 recorded observations in the region, spotting one would be a significant addition to a birder's life list.
compareHints: Cave Swallows are most similar to Cliff Swallows, sharing the same genus, but Cave Swallows have that diagnostic square tail versus the Cliff Swallow's notched or slightly forked tail. Cave Swallows also show more rufous coloring on the rump and have a buffer, less contrasted throat pattern. While Cliff Swallows are common summer residents in New England, Cave Swallows appear only as rare vagrants.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cave Swallows, the only other species in the same genus that occasionally appears in New England, have a rust-colored throat and forehead instead of the Cliff Swallow's pale forehead and dark throat.
